where: the blue '+' quick-add button, floating over the right edge of the list at roughly two-thirds down the screen
finding: The counselor's thumb rests on the one pixel where three different actions collide. The quick-add FAB is `fixed`, so at every scroll position it sits on top of the right-hand edge of two student rows — and the point a right thumb naturally lands on is the seam between them. A tap that lands there does one of three things depending on 8px of error: check the next student in, undo the last student's check-in, or throw up a full-screen 'Add a visitor' dialog on top of a queue. The dialog case is the dangerous one, because the counselor aimed at a student's check circle, saw something happen, dismissed it, and moved on — and that student is not checked in.
evidence: The FAB is `fixed bottom-safe-bottom right-4 mb-20 size-14 z-30` → a 56×56 box at x 318–374, y 708–764 CSS. In this frame Layla Farouk's row (undo) occupies y 668–733 and Noah Fitzgerald's row (check in) occupies y 740–805, both spanning x 12–378. The FAB's centre, (346, 736), is 3px from the seam between them. Its box covers y 708–733 of Layla's row and y 740–764 of Noah's — including the top of Noah's 24px check indicator, which is centred at (354, 772) and is the only visual affordance the row offers. The same collision appears in roster-search, where the FAB lands on Aisha Rahman's row at y 740.
direction: Nothing about the FAB's job requires it to be over the list. The `mb-20` is lifting it 80px off the bottom of a screen that has no bottom bar on this scene, which is what pushes it into the rows in the first place. Either drop it to the bottom edge and let the list end above it (extra bottom padding on the list rather than a floating overlay), or move quick-add out of the scroll plane entirely — it belongs next to search, since 'this person isn't in the list' is a search outcome, not a scrolling one.

where: the CATCH UP list occupying the bottom half of the screen, versus the 'Start check-in' hero at the top
finding: Every target inside a counselor's thumb arc opens the wrong night's register. The one action they came for — start tonight — sits at y 299–355, which needs a grip shift on a 844px phone; the five things they can reach without one are all past gatherings, and two of them are titled 'Friday Fellowship' exactly like tonight's. A counselor who taps the wrong Friday in a dim hallway does not get an error; they get a roster that looks identical and start filing forty-five students against last week's date. That is the wrong-data failure, and the layout puts the risky targets where the thumb is and the safe one where it is not.
evidence: Hero `<a>` at (16,129) 358×246 CSS, with the 'Start check-in' block at y 299–355. The catch-up rows are 358×64 at y 467, 539, 611, 683, 755 — three of them sit wholly inside the bottom third (563–844), and 'Friday Fellowship · Fri 24' at y 539 shares its title with the hero. Once opened, the only thing on the roster screen distinguishing tonight from Fri 24 is a 12px 'Today · 3:12 PM – 5:12 PM' line and an 11px 'Today' chip at y 112. Total page height is 947px, so the whole screen is a single flick — there is no scroll cost to reordering it.
direction: Invert the vertical priority: tonight's card belongs in the reachable zone and 'Catch up' belongs above it or behind a disclosure, since it is a deliberate, once-in-a-while intent, not a hallway one. Failing that, the past-register roster needs to announce its date at the weight the hero uses, not at 11–12px, so a wrong tap is caught on the first student rather than the forty-fifth.

where: the whole fold — Quick add card, TODAY hero, and the first NEXT SEVEN DAYS row clipped by the bottom nav
finding: Two of the three things this scene exists for cannot be started on the fold. 'See what is on' returns zero complete upcoming rows, because 190px at the top is spent on two green ticks confirming work that is already done and another 246px on a hero card duplicating the counselor's choose-event screen. 'Find the gathering from three weeks ago' is worse: the past list begins 2,541px down, behind fourteen future gatherings running out to Sep 20, with no search and no jump — roughly six thumb flicks to reach a date the leader could have named out loud.
evidence: Quick add rows at (28,224) and (28,288), both reading '✓ … is scheduled'; the TODAY hero is 358×246 at (16,412); the first upcoming row is at (16,714) 358×93 and the bottom nav starts at y 776, so 62 of its 93px show and the next row at y 815 is entirely below the fold. Upcoming rows run y 714–2470 (14 rows × 93px). The first past row, 'Sunday School · Sun 26', is at y 2541; 'Load older gatherings' is at y 3441 on a 3,686px page. No search field or date jump exists anywhere on the scene.
direction: The past is the half of this page that gets hunted through, and it is the half that is furthest away. Give the fold a way in — a period switch (upcoming / past) or a jump to today's position in one continuous list — and collapse the 'already scheduled' confirmations into a single line so the calendar itself starts above the fold.

where: every phone frame in this round, most visibly the roster search field at y 164
finding: The phone frames are being rendered as a fine-pointer device, so the component library's desktop compactions are applied to the screenshots both critics are judging. Right now that only shifts the roster by 11px, so this round's conclusions still hold — but the whole point of the coming rounds is to widen the gap between touch and pointer via `pointer-fine:` variants, and every one of those edits will show up in the phone frames as the *pointer* version. The loop would then converge on a phone design nobody has actually looked at.
evidence: `uxr/shoot.ts` builds the phone context with `viewport: {390,844}, deviceScaleFactor: 2` and no `hasTouch`/`isMobile`, so Chromium reports `pointer: fine`. The frozen CSS carries `@media (pointer: fine) { input, select, textarea { font-size: 14px } }` plus the `pointer-fine:*` utilities. In the shipped frame the search input measures 366×37 CSS at 14px; re-rendering the same file with `hasTouch: true, isMobile: true` gives 366×48 at 16px, and every row below it moves down 11px. Separately, the `-full` phone frames are byte-identical to `-fold` (all 780×1688) even though roster is 2,183px and events 3,686px tall, so the full-page frames currently carry no information.
direction: Add `hasTouch: true, isMobile: true` to the phone context in `uxr/shoot.ts` and re-shoot before the ideator acts on anything, and check why full-page capture is collapsing to viewport height — likely the `h-full` root plus `min-h-dvh` making `document.scrollHeight` equal the viewport.

where: the Missing in action rows, and the red 'MISSED' badge at the right of each
finding: The loudest thing in each MIA row is not tappable and the tappable thing is a text block in the middle. A leader thumbing down the list to open Leila Haddad's record aims at the red '5 MISSED' badge — the only saturated element in the row — and gets nothing. Recoverable in one retry, but it happens on all ten rows, and only two of them fit above the fold to begin with.
evidence: Each row's `<a>` measures 206×56 CSS starting at x 84; the row itself spans x 12–378. The 44px avatar to its left and the ~72px danger-tinted badge to its right are outside the link, leaving 44% of the row's width dead. First MIA link is at y 610, second at y 711, and the bottom nav starts at y 776 — two of ten visible. Each row also spends a 24px line on a 'Looking up contact details…' spinner, so about a quarter of every row is a placeholder for the phone number this screen exists to produce.
direction: Make the whole row the target — the badge and avatar have no competing action — and let the contact line resolve into something tappable (a `tel:` link) rather than a spinner, since 'who to phone' ends in a phone call.

where: the 'INCOMPLETE' stat tile, bottom-right of the 2×2 grid
finding: One of the three questions the dashboard is for — who nobody can reach — reads as an em dash. A leader glancing at 'INCOMPLETE / — / no parent contact' cannot tell whether that means none, or not loaded, and will read it as 'nothing to do here'. The app knows the answer: the Students scene two taps away offers an 'Incomplete profiles (5)' filter.
evidence:
The tile renders `

—

` in the same slot where the neighbouring tiles print 16, 10 and 2. The Students phone frame shows a chip labelled 'Incomplete profiles (5)' at (16,349).
direction: Show the number, and make the tile carry the same tap-through the Students chip does. If it is genuinely pending, a skeleton reads as pending; an em dash reads as zero.

where: the header block above the list, and the hairline dividers between rows
finding: Half the screen belongs to something other than the list of students. The two largest, brightest targets — 'Add from Planning Center' filling 61% of the width in solid brand blue, and 'New visitor' below it — are admin actions a leader takes rarely, and they push the first name to y 409, leaving six of forty-five students visible. Search rescues the job when the leader knows the name, which is why this is friction rather than failure, but browsing costs seven and a half flicks where it could cost four.
evidence: 'Add from Planning Center' is 237×44 at (137,65) and 'New visitor' 121×44 at (253,117) — 96px of vertical space for two rare actions, above a 358×48 search field at y 203. First row at (16,409) 358×64; bottom nav at y 776; six full rows fit. Rows are `divide-y divide-ink-800` with a 65px pitch on a 64px row, so adjacent students are separated by a 1px hairline and no gap — an 8px miss opens the wrong record. The roster's equivalent list uses `gap-2` between the same-height rows.
direction: Demote the two import actions to a single secondary control (they are not what anyone opened this screen for) and give the directory rows the roster's spacing so the tap boundaries are visible, not just implied.

where: the bottom navigation bar, Events and Students tabs
finding: The two right-hand nav tabs are near-identical glyphs, flush against each other, sitting in the thumb zone. '▤' and '☰' differ by one horizontal rule at a glance, and the 11px labels underneath are below the size that survives a glance in a dim room. The two tabs go to entirely different places, and there is no gap between their hit boxes.
evidence: Nav items measure 98×56 CSS at x 0, 98, 195 and 293, y 776 — abutting, zero gap. Labels render at 11px. The icons are single characters: ✓, ◎, ▤, ☰.
direction: The app deliberately has no icon library, so the fix is glyph choice rather than iconography — pick two characters that differ in silhouette (a calendar-ish and a person-ish mark) and raise the labels to at least 12px, since the label is doing most of the discriminating work anyway.

where: the Missing in action card, from y=318 to the bottom edge, inside the 481px content column that sits between the 224px nav rail and 367px of empty page
finding: The leader opens Insights on a Tuesday to answer one question — who do I phone this week — and the answer is a list of 10 names. Three of them are readable without scrolling; the fourth (Rohan Desai) is sliced by the 900px fold. Every name they act on after the third costs a scroll, and because the phone number and the Call/Text buttons live inside each card rather than in a column, they cannot skim the list to plan the evening: they scroll, read, scroll back. The list is the job, and one third of one screen of it is showing.
evidence: Content column is max-w-lg (32rem) with px-4, measured 592→1073 = 481px in a 1440px window; the rail ends at x=222, so 735px of the 1216px content region — 60% — is empty page. MIA rows are 114–125px tall (row tops at y=406, 530, 644, 769) and carry eight facts each: initials, name, grade, last-seen date, which gathering, missed count, phone, two buttons. Ten of them is roughly 1,200px of column, and MIA is only the first of six stacked sections (MIA 10, New faces 2, Attendance trend, Incomplete profiles 7, One-off events, Met once never since 2) — about 3,400px, near four screens.
direction: At lg: let the column take the region it is standing in, and turn the MIA card into rows the width of the window: name, grade, missing-from, missed count, last seen, phone, actions as columns at 48–56px per row. All ten names then fit under the tiles above the fold. Nothing here needs the gathering split to change — the All/Sunday/Friday control keeps working on a wide table.

where: sections stacked below the MIA card — New faces, Attendance trend, Incomplete profiles, One-off events, Met once never since — all in the same 481px column
finding: The brief names three questions for this screen: who drifted, who is new, who nobody can reach. Only the first has any presence above the fold. 'Who is new' (2 names) sits behind ~1,200px of MIA rows, and 'who nobody can reach' (7 names) sits behind that plus the whole attendance trend chart and its 8-row table. These are two-name and seven-name lists — they are small, and they are stacked in single file behind the big one for no reason other than that the layout was built for a 390px phone.
evidence: Every section is a child of the same mx-auto max-w-lg flex-col, so they can only stack. New faces is 2 rows, Incomplete profiles is 7 rows at ~70px, One-off events is 1 row, Met once never since is 2 rows — together under 900px of content occupying nearly 2,000px of scroll. Meanwhile 735px of horizontal space is unused on every one of those screens.
direction: At lg: two columns. MIA stays the wide left column because it is the long list; New faces, Incomplete profiles and Met once never since stack in a narrower right column beside it, with the trend chart below. Three of the leader's questions get answered in one screenful instead of four.

where: the INCOMPLETE stat tile (fourth tile, top right of the content column) versus the 'Incomplete profiles (5)' filter chip on the students screen
finding: The tile says 7 with the caption 'no parent contact', and the dashboard's own Incomplete profiles section repeats 7 and describes it as 'Active students with no parent phone or email on file.' The students screen — one click away in the rail, and the place a leader goes to fix this — offers a chip labelled 'Incomplete profiles (5)'. Same words, same stated scope (the Status filter already reads Active), different number. On desktop the rail puts both numbers within one click of each other, so the leader will see the mismatch, and their next thought is which one is lying, on the exact screen whose value is that its counts can be trusted.
evidence: dashboard--desktop.html: tile 'Incomplete / 7 / no parent contact' and section header 'Incomplete profiles 7 — Active students with no parent phone or email on file', listing Selah Mbeki, Jayden Rivers, Bree Sandoval, Tomas Vielle, Kylie Novak, Kai Alofa, Trevor Boyd. students--desktop.html: chip 'Incomplete profiles (5)' with the Status select defaulted to Active; only the five visitors carry a Missing info badge in the list — Kai Alofa and Trevor Boyd do not.
direction: One definition, one number, both places. If the students chip is deliberately visitors-only, it needs a different word — the dashboard's number is the one the leader is acting on, and the two should land on the same seven names when clicked through.

where: the whole page: Quick add card, the Today hero, 'NEXT SEVEN DAYS', and the 'LATER' heading sitting empty at y=866
finding: One of the three jobs on this screen is 'find the gathering from three weeks ago'. On a 1440x900 laptop that means scrolling past a 225px hero card for an event happening right now — which the leader already knows about, and which is also the whole of the choose-event screen — then past 16 future occurrences of two recurring series, before the Past gatherings heading appears roughly 2,500px down, about three screens. The screen shows 2 of its 27 gatherings above the fold. A month is a shape a pointer screen is unusually good at showing and this one never draws it, so the leader navigates a date problem by scrolling a list.
evidence: Content column is max-w-3xl minus px-4, measured 464→1200 = 736px; 480px of the 1216px region beside the rail is empty. Today's hero card runs y=353→578 (225px) for a single event. Upcoming rows are ~93px (Jul 31 at 634→727, Aug 2 at 735→827); the markup holds 2 rows under Next seven days, 16 under Later, then Past gatherings with 9 July entries. 16 x 93 = ~1,490px of future before any past appears.
direction: At lg: a month grid in the space that is already empty, with the list beside or beneath it, so three weeks ago is a click on a date rather than a scroll. Keep the constraint in view — calendar cells carry the gathering name and time only, no RSVP or head counts. Collapse the Today hero to a single row at this width; it is a duplicate of the check-in entry point, not a landing card.

where: the student list starting at y=279, 640px wide, in the region right of the 224px rail
finding: The job is 'find one student among forty-five, see who has no parent contact, open a record'. Nine names are visible; scanning the directory takes three and a half screens. Each 65px row spends about 250px on initials, name and grade and leaves the remaining 390px — 61% of the row — empty, then puts a chevron at the far right of that emptiness. The 'who has no parent contact' half of the job is only answerable by clicking a filter chip, which discards the alphabetical view the leader was using, when the flag could simply be a column that is always readable.
evidence: Column is max-w-2xl minus px-4, measured 512→1152 = 640px inside a 1216px region — 576px unused. Rows are min-h-16 (65px pitch: Aisha at 279, Amara at 344, Ana Lucia at 409); 622px of list below the y=278 filter block holds 9 full rows and a sliver of Diego Herrera, of 45 students. Only three rows in the whole list carry a Missing info badge inline (Bree Sandoval, Jayden Rivers, Kylie Novak).
direction: At lg: full-width rows at ~44px and columns for what is already on this screen or the dashboard — grade, visitor flag, missing-contact flag, last seen. Twenty-plus names above the fold and the incomplete ones legible without filtering. The brief forbids inventing richer student cards, so the fix is columns for facts the app already displays, not new fields about a minor.

where: the roster list below y=268, in a 744px column with 348px of empty page on each side
finding: Forty-five students, nine names on screen. When check-in is run from a laptop at a table rather than a phone at a door, the leader is scrolling a 3,200px list to find a name they can see is nowhere near the top, in a window where nearly half the width is blank. Before the first name there is 212px of chrome — event card, Today/Change, the date select, the search field, the Recent/Checked in chips — a quarter of the window spent on things read once.
evidence: Column is max-w-3xl, measured 348→1092 = 744px of 1440; rows are 72px pitch (Maya at 302, Andre at 374, Chloe at 446); nine names visible with Diego Herrera cut at the fold, out of 45. Header block runs y=56→268. roster-search shows the same geometry: 'ma' returns 9 results and they exactly fill the screen, so any query looser than two letters starts scrolling too.
direction: At lg: two or three columns of the same A-Z list, and a single-row header bar instead of a stacked one. This does not touch the constraint — the sort never changes and a check-in still recolours a row where it stands; the row simply has neighbours to its side as well as below. Thirty names above the fold instead of nine.

where: the four stat tiles at y=160–305 and the 'Copy list' button in the Missing in action header
finding: On a 1440px laptop, a two-word button wraps to two lines and a tile caption wraps to three. Nothing is unreadable, but it is the tell that this column was sized for a phone: the leader's eye has to reassemble 'Sunday School · -2 vs 18 before' across three lines and 'Copy list' across two, at the top of the screen where they are trying to take in four numbers at a glance.
evidence: sm:grid-cols-4 inside the 481px column gives each tile ~112px: 'LAST GATHERING' breaks after LAST, its caption runs three lines (y=245–290), 'MIA' caption '3+ missed in a row' runs two, 'INCOMPLETE' fills its tile width edge to edge. The Copy list button at x=973–1057 renders as 'Copy' over 'list'.
direction: Falls out of the wider column: four tiles across 1,216px are ~290px each and every caption fits one line, and the header button stops wrapping. No type-size change needed — this is a width problem, not a density one.

where: the Catch up rows — the green attendance count against the gathering name
finding: In every catch-up row the loudest element is the historical head-count, not the gathering it belongs to. The count is text-xl font-bold in present-400; the event name beside it is a plain base-size semibold in ink-100 — a step smaller and a step further from the reader. Squint at the lower half of the frame and you read '16 24 18 26 21' as a column, and the names only afterwards. Worse, the accent is borrowed: present is the app's word for 'this student is checked in', and here it is spent on a total from a night that is over. The reader picks a row by its name and its date, and both of those are the quiet part.
evidence: choose-event--phone-fold.png, the five rows below CATCH UP: green numerals sit a full type step above the titles they annotate, and use the same green as the checked-in rows in roster--phone-fold.png.
direction: Invert the emphasis inside the row: the gathering name and its date are the thing being chosen and should be the heaviest ink in the row; the past count is context and belongs at the weight of the date line, in neutral ink rather than present. Reserve present for live check-in state so the token keeps one meaning across the app.

where: the event header block — H1, subtitle, 'Today' badge, 'Change' link and the date select
finding: Which gathering you are on is stated four times in the top 200px, in four different visual idioms, and the two controls that change it are dressed as unrelated things. The H1 says Friday Fellowship; the line under it says 'Today · 3:12 PM…'; a chip repeats 'Today'; and a pill select repeats 'Jul 27 · Friday Fellow…' truncated. Next to it 'Change' is a bare blue word with a 44px hit area and no boundary — it reads as body text, while the select next to it reads as the control. Two affordances for one question, plus a badge that restates a word already on screen: the block reads as assembled from three separate ideas rather than composed as one header.
evidence: roster--phone-fold.png and roster-search--phone-fold.png, the two rows between the app bar and the search field. 'Today' appears twice, 'Friday Fellow…' twice, and the select is truncated while the H1 above it has room.
direction: Decide that the header states the gathering once and offers exactly one way to change it. Let the title line carry identity and time; drop the badge that repeats a word from the line above; and collapse 'Change' and the select into a single control with one visual weight, so the row has a subject and a verb rather than three competing chips.

where: the INCOMPLETE stat tile in the four-up grid
finding: Three tiles carry tabular numerals and the fourth carries an em dash, so the row of answers has a hole in it. A dash where its neighbours have digits reads as 'not measured', which is the one thing it is not: the Incomplete profiles section further down the same page carries a count pill of 5. The tile that exists to answer 'who has nobody we can reach' is the tile that appears to have failed to load, and it contradicts the page under it.
evidence: dashboard--phone-full.png: tile reads INCOMPLETE / — / no parent contact, while the 'Incomplete profiles' section header on the same page reads 'Incomplete profiles 5'.
direction: The tile should show the same figure as the section it summarises, set in the same tabular numeral as its three neighbours, and take the same semantic tint the other alarming tile takes when the number is non-zero. Keep the dash only for a genuinely unavailable measure — and if a real zero can occur, a zero is a number and should be printed as one.

where: the page header — 'Students / 45 students' against the two action buttons
finding: The loudest object on a page whose job is finding one student among forty-five is a brand-filled 'Add from Planning Center' button — a bulk import someone does twice a year. It is wide enough to claim the entire first line, which wraps 'New visitor' onto a second line, so the header is a two-row staircase of buttons beside a two-line title, and the search field — the actual instrument of the page — starts 300 device px down. Hierarchy is exactly inverted: the rare administrative action wears the accent, the constant action wears a form label.
evidence: students--phone-fold.png: the brand fill occupies the top-right quadrant, 'New visitor' is orphaned on its own line below it, and 'Search' does not appear until roughly a third of the way down the fold.
direction: Only one thing in this header should carry the brand fill and it should be the one a leader does weekly. Demote the import to the quiet weight the secondary button has now, or move it out of the header entirely; and let the header be one line so the search field rises into the first screen.

where: the 'Quick add' card and its two rows
finding: The card is titled 'Quick add' and subtitled 'Next occurrence of each series', but its rows are dressed as completed items: a green tick on the left, and a label that says 'Friday Fellowship is scheduled' set in ink-300 rather than the ink-50/ink-100 every other list row in the app uses for its primary label. A tick plus a past-tense statement plus dimmed ink is the universal costume for 'done, nothing to do here'. So the one card on the page that is offering an action reads as a receipt for an action already taken, and the reader's eye skips it on the way to the real content.
evidence: events--phone-fold.png: both rows inside Quick add show '✓ … is scheduled' in dimmed text, visually identical to a completed checklist, sitting under a header that promises an add.
direction: Pick one story for this card and dress it consistently. If these are still actions, the label should be the thing you would create and the row should carry the ink and the affordance of a live control; if they are confirmations of something already scheduled, the card should not be called Quick add. Either way the dimmed ink is doing damage — a row you are meant to tap should not sit two steps back from the reader.

where: the floating '+' button where it lands over the Noah Fitzgerald row
finding: The add-a-visitor button floats with no relationship to anything on the page and comes to rest directly on top of a row's check circle, with no gutter, no scrim and no shadow to separate the planes. Because the circle it covers is exactly the affordance the whole screen is built around, the row underneath reads as a partially drawn or unavailable one, and the composition acquires a collision at its busiest point — the right-hand column where every row's state lives.
evidence: roster--phone-fold.png: the blue disc spans roughly x 318–373, y 708–763 CSS px, covering the ring on the Noah Fitzgerald row; the same collision recurs on the Aisha Rahman row in roster-search--phone-fold.png.
direction: The floating control needs to belong to the page's structure rather than hover in the middle of it — give the list enough trailing space that the button never sits over a row's state column, and give the button a visible separation from the plane below so the two never read as one broken row.

where: the uppercase section headings (TODAY, NEXT SEVEN DAYS, CATCH UP, RECENT) against the cards beneath them
finding: Every section heading carries a small horizontal inset that its cards do not, so no heading shares a left edge with the block it labels — the text starts about 4–5 CSS px inboard of the card edge below it. It is too small to read as a deliberate offset and too consistent to read as an accident; the effect is a page where nothing quite lines up and the eye finds no spine. On choose-event the heading sits at x 20 while the card edge sits at x 15.
evidence: choose-event--phone-fold.png ('On today' and 'CATCH UP' both inset from the card edges) and events--phone-fold.png ('TODAY' and 'NEXT SEVEN DAYS' likewise); the markup gives the headings a px-1 the cards do not have.
direction: Put the headings on the same left edge as the cards they introduce so a single vertical line runs the length of every page. If a heading is meant to sit outside the card gutter, make the offset large enough to read as a choice rather than a rounding error.

where: the secondary line in each roster row — the allergy badge and the 'x of 3' ratio
finding: The attendance ratio is set in tabular numerals, which says someone wanted it to line up, and then its column moves: on rows with an allergy badge the badge is laid out first and pushes '3 of 3' about 75 CSS px to the right. Scanning the list, the one number you compare between students never appears twice in the same place, so the tabular setting buys nothing. The badge also drops the loudest colour in the row into the quietest line, so an amber chip is heavier than the student's own name.
evidence: roster--phone-fold.png: '3 of 3' begins at the same x on Maya, Chloe, Ruby and Marcus, then jumps right on the Layla Farouk and Noah Fitzgerald rows where the Allergy chip precedes it.
direction: Give the ratio a fixed position in the row — either always first on the meta line with badges trailing it, or in its own column — so it forms a readable vertical run. And let the allergy flag be legible without out-shouting the name; a warning in the third-rank line should not be the heaviest mark in the row.

where: the 'Check-in open' badge and the 'Check-in is open' caption beside it
finding: The same sentence is printed twice, side by side, once loud and once quiet. A ringed green chip saying 'Check-in open' sits immediately left of grey text saying 'Check-in is open'. Neither adds anything to the other, and the pair makes the reader stop and check whether they are two different facts. It also puts a third piece of present-green into a card that already carries a brand-filled primary button, so the status line competes with the action beneath it for no return.
evidence: choose-event--phone-fold.png and events--phone-fold.png, the row directly above 'Start check-in' / 'Open this gathering'.
direction: Say it once. Either the chip carries the status and the caption goes, or the caption carries it and the chip goes — and whichever survives should sit at a weight that lets the primary button remain the loudest thing in the card.

where: the Missing in action rows and the filter chip row above the stat tiles
finding: Two things keep the top of this page from settling. The filter chips wrap to two lines and orphan 'Friday Fellowship' alone on the second, so the fold opens on a ragged block of controls that is taller than any of the numbers it filters. And each MIA row has three different left edges: the name and its meta line align, then 'Looking up contact details…' starts further right again, a third indent inside a row only four lines tall. In the same rows 'Last seen Jun 21, 1…' truncates mid-value while the line directly beneath it uses barely half its width — the fact is cut off in a place where there was room.
evidence: dashboard--phone-fold.png: the chip group runs two rows before the tiles begin; on the Leila Haddad and Trevor Boyd rows the third line is indented past the two above it and both 'Last seen' dates end in an ellipsis mid-time.
direction: Let the chip row stay on one line so the fold opens on the numbers rather than the filters. Inside a row, hold every line to one left edge unless the indent means something. And rebalance what the meta lines carry so a date is never truncated while the line under it is half empty — grade, last-seen and which gathering are three facts competing for one line's worth of width.

where: the page frame — sidebar, content column, and the voids either side of it
finding: The sidebar is pinned hard to the left edge and the content is a 480px column centred in the 1218px that remains, so there is a 370px void between the nav and the thing it navigates and another 368px to its right. The column is not just narrow, it is unanchored: it aligns to nothing, least of all the sidebar. And the measure is not even shared across the section — Events runs at 736px and Students at 640px, so the content's left edge jumps 592 → 464 → 512 as you move between three tabs whose sidebar never moves. Three pages that are obviously siblings read as three unrelated documents that happen to share furniture, and every one of them is a phone column parked in the middle of a laptop.
evidence: The subtitle breaks to a second line to orphan the single word 'gathering'. 'Copy list' — two short words — wraps to two lines inside its own button. All four MIA meta lines truncate mid-word ('at Sund…', 'at Sunda…', 'at Frida…', 'at Friday …'), each at a different point, producing a ragged column of ellipses while 368px of the window is painted flat ink-950. The four stat tiles are squeezed to 118px each so their labels wrap.
direction: Stop centring. Give the whole core-team section one page frame: content begins at a fixed gutter from the sidebar's edge and runs to a fixed right gutter, so the left edge is constant across Insights, Events and Students and the sidebar reads as attached to the page. Spend the recovered width on columns — the stat row and the MIA list are two blocks that can sit side by side rather than stacked — not on a wider single measure.

where: the four stat tiles beneath the gathering filter
finding: Three of the four tiles carry a saturated accent wash — danger on MIA, present on New faces, warn on Incomplete — sitting shoulder to shoulder in one 480px row. When three quarters of a row is accented, the accent has stopped being a signal and become a decoration scheme: the good news (2 new faces, green) shouts exactly as loudly as the thing that put you on this page (10 missing, red). Nothing in the row is allowed to be more urgent than anything else, which on a screen whose entire job is 'who do I phone this week' is the composition arguing against the content.
evidence: Four tiles, four different backgrounds — one neutral ink-900 and three tinted at equal strength. Read at a squint the row is a stripe of red-green-amber with no dominant, and the eye lands on the leftmost neutral tile ('Last gathering, 16') by default, which is the one fact that requires no action.
direction: Let one tile carry the accent — the one that is actually a call to action — and set the rest on the neutral ink surface, using the accent only on the numeral or a hairline rather than the whole field. The tints are the right tokens; the mistake is applying all of them at once.

where: the numerals inside the four stat tiles
finding: The four big numbers do not share a baseline. 'Last gathering' wraps its label to two lines while MIA, New faces and Incomplete keep theirs on one, so 16 sits about 16px lower than 10 and 2, and 7 sits higher still. These four figures exist to be compared at a glance, and a row of comparable quantities that steps up and down reads as four separate boxes rather than one instrument.
evidence: 16 lands at roughly y=225, 10 and 2 at y=209, 7 at y=197. The captions beneath run to three lines, two lines and one line respectively, so the tiles' internal rhythm differs in every cell.
direction: Fix the label to one line (a wider frame does most of this for free) and align the numerals to a shared baseline, letting the captions hang from a common line below. The tiles should read as one ruled row, not four independently packed cards.

where: the two meta lines under each name in Missing in action
finding: Each row carries two lines of identical size, colour and weight, and the second is a restatement of the tail of the first — '…1 month ago at Sunday School' followed by 'Missing from Sunday School'. Because the first line truncates, the reader loses the words that the second line then repeats in full, so the block reads as one sentence stuttering rather than as two facts. Two lines at the same value also means neither is subordinate, and the name above them has to fight both.
evidence: '11th grade · Last seen Jun 21, 1 month ago at Sund…' / 'Missing from Sunday School' on Leila Haddad; the same doubling on all four visible rows. Both lines are the same dim grey at the same size.
direction: One meta line per row. If the gathering must appear twice, differentiate the two lines — one is identity and history, one is the reason this person is in this list — by weight or position, or fold the gathering into the missed-count chip on the right, which already has room.

where: the two rows inside the Quick add card
finding: These are the page's shortcut to scheduling next week, and they are dressed as receipts for work already done: a green check in the `present` accent leads a title in past tense — 'Friday Fellowship is scheduled' — set in a dimmer grey than any other card title on the page. Green tick plus past-participle plus dimmed text is the universal costume of a completed item, so the one control that saves a leader the most time reads as a log entry. The card's own heading says 'Quick add'; nothing beneath it looks addable.
evidence: Both rows are `present-400` ✓ + `ink-300` title, against `ink-50` titles on every other row on the page. They also carry no right-hand chevron, while the 'Next seven days' rows directly below them do — so the rows that are actions look less interactive than the rows that are merely records.
direction: Make these read as the affordance they are: title at full ink-50, copy in the imperative rather than the passive, and either a leading glyph that means 'add' or none at all — the `present` check belongs to students who turned up, not to a button. Give them the same chevron as the rows below, or take the chevron off both.

where: 'Quick add' against 'TODAY' / 'NEXT SEVEN DAYS' / 'LATER'
finding: The page runs two incompatible systems for the same rank of heading. 'Quick add' is 16px bold sentence case with a 14px explainer, sitting inside a ringed card; the three date groups are 11px uppercase tracked dim grey with nothing around them. Structurally these are peers — four groups of event rows down one page — but the treatments say one is a parent and three are captions, so the eye reads the page as one big block followed by loose debris.
evidence: Four section heads, two type systems, and the loudest of them belongs to the smallest group (two rows) while 'TODAY', which owns the largest and most important card, is the quietest thing above it.
direction: Pick one voice for section headings on this page and use it four times. If Quick add genuinely outranks the date groups, express that with the container, not by giving its heading a different typeface altogether.

where: the 'Open this gathering' button in the Today card
finding: A 704px-wide, 52px-tall solid blue bar is by a wide margin the heaviest object on a page whose job is scanning a calendar. It is a phone's full-bleed primary action grown to fill a desktop card rather than composed for one — at this size the button is no longer a control, it is a horizontal rule painted brand blue, and it cuts the card in half so the event's own details read as a caption above it.
evidence: The bar spans the entire inner width of the card and is taller and more saturated than the card title 'Friday Fellowship'. It also out-weighs 'New event' at the top of the page, which is the action a leader actually came here for on a Tuesday morning.
direction: At pointer widths let the primary action size to its label and sit on a line with the card's metadata rather than spanning it, so the card reads title-first. The full-bleed treatment is right on the phone and should stay there.

where: the header row — title, 'Add from Planning Center', 'New visitor' — against the search field below
finding: The loudest, widest, most saturated object on this screen is a bulk-import button. It is 236px of filled brand blue, wider than the page title next to it and heavier than anything in the list, and it sits in the top-right corner where the eye lands first. The job of this screen is finding one student among forty-five; that job's control is a quiet outlined box below, indistinguishable from the two dropdowns under it. The hierarchy is exactly inverted — the rarest action is the biggest, and the constant one is furniture.
evidence: 'Add from Planning Center' is the only filled-blue element on the page and is visibly wider than the 'Students' h1 beside it. The search input directly beneath carries the same ring, radius and fill as the Grade and Status selects, so nothing marks it as the primary way in.
direction: Demote the import to the same quiet treatment as 'New visitor' — it is an occasional administrative act, not the page's purpose — and let the search field carry the visual weight instead, either by size or by sitting alone on its line above the two filters that qualify it.

where: the search/filter block and the right edge of the list rows
finding: The filter stack has a staircase right edge: the search input runs the full 640px measure, the Grade and Status selects stop 216px short of it, and the two chips below stop shorter still. Three consecutive rows, three different right terminations, none of them a deliberate-looking choice — it reads as controls dropped in at their natural widths rather than a set. Below that, every list row carries two short left-aligned facts and a chevron pinned to the far right with roughly 400px of nothing between them, so the chevron floats unmoored rather than closing the row.
evidence: Search input ends at x≈1152, the Status select at x≈936, 'Visitors (5)' at x≈805. In the list, 'Aisha Rahman / 7th grade' ends near x=707 and the chevron sits at x=1136.
direction: Make the filter block a set: either align all three rows to the same right edge or let the selects share the input's line as a single toolbar. In the rows, either bring more fact out to meet the chevron — this is a wide screen and the row is carrying two words — or let the row close where its content ends.

where: the green attendance count on every Catch up row
finding: In each of the five catch-up rows the loudest element is the number on the right: 20px bold in the `present` green, against an event name set at 16px semibold in plain ink. The thing you tap — which gathering — is quieter than a historical total you cannot act on, so the list reads as a table of scores with the names as labels. The colour compounds it: `present` means a student is checked in right now, and here it is being spent on a closed count from three weeks ago, which teaches the reader that green means nothing in particular.
evidence: '16', '24', '18', '26', '21' are the first things visible when the frame is squinted; the names 'Sunday School' and 'Friday Fellowship' arrive second. Five green numerals in a stack out-weigh the one green pill above them ('Check-in open') that describes a genuinely live state.
direction: Invert the weights — the gathering name and date are what is being chosen and should arrive first; the count is a footnote and should read as one. Keep the number, drop the accent, or reserve the green for the row that is actually open.

where: the 'Check-in open' pill and the grey text immediately to its right
finding: The same fact is stated twice, adjacent, in two different treatments: a green ringed pill reading 'Check-in open' followed 8px later by dim grey text reading 'Check-in is open'. Two objects, one fact — which forces the reader to check whether the second is qualifying the first, find that it is not, and move on. The grey restatement also drains the pill: a badge next to a sentence saying the same thing reads like a label for the sentence rather than a status.
evidence: Both fragments sit on one flex line under the event description; the pill is `present` tinted, the text is `ink-500`.
direction: One of them. The pill alone is enough at this size; if a sentence is wanted, let it say something the pill cannot — until when, or how many are in already.

where: the 'On today' and 'CATCH UP' section headings
finding: The two sections are structurally identical — a heading followed by one line of explanatory copy followed by a list — and are rendered in two entirely different systems: 'On today' at 20px bold sentence case with a 14px explainer, 'CATCH UP' at 11px uppercase tracked grey with a 12px explainer. The parallel structure sets up an expectation of peers and the typography contradicts it, so the second section reads as an appendix to the first rather than the other of two choices.
evidence: The two heading blocks are ~10px apart in size and three steps apart in weight and case, while their sub-lines sit at the same rhythm beneath each.
direction: Give the two sections the same heading treatment and let the difference in importance be carried by what is under them — one card at full weight versus five quiet rows already does that work.

where: the rule under the filter chip band, and the rule under the top bar
finding: The filter band's bottom border runs the full 1440px of the window while everything inside it stops at a centred 768px column. The rule therefore draws a full-width layout the page never delivers, and the 336px of it that extends past the chips on either side underlines nothing at all. It is the most explicit statement on the screen that this composition was designed for a narrower window and then let out.
evidence: The divider at y≈267 crosses the whole frame; the rightmost content above it ('All grades') ends at x=1092 and the leftmost ('Recent') begins at x=348. The header rule above behaves the same way, though there the wordmark and account chip at least reach both ends.
direction: Either let the rule end with its content, or give the band content that reaches the rule. The second is the better answer on a pointer screen — the roster has width to spend and the band is where the spending should start.

where: the 'Today' chip, the 'Change' link and the date select, all on one 40px band
finding: One decision — which gathering am I taking the register for — is offered three ways in a single row, in three visual languages: a small grey capsule, a blue text link, and a large ringed select that is the only browser-chrome control anywhere in the frame. The select's radius, its chevron and its type all come from somewhere other than this design system, and at 226px × 41px it is also the heaviest object in the band, which puts the most weight on the least urgent decision on a screen where the queue is waiting.
evidence: The 22px-tall 'Today' chip and the 41px-tall select share a baseline row but differ by nearly 2× in height and by three treatments in style; 'Change' sits between them as unaccompanied blue text.
direction: Collapse this to one control with one treatment. Whichever survives should be built from the same chip/button vocabulary as the filter row below it so the header band reads as one set of controls rather than three imported ones.

where: the filter row once a query is active
finding: With 'ma' typed, the 'Recent 24' chip vanishes and 'Checked in' slides left into the space it left, so the row that was a two-chip group becomes a single chip on the far left and 'All grades' stranded on the far right with roughly 500px of empty band between them. The row no longer reads as a group of anything — it reads as two controls that happen to share a line. The band above it thins at the same moment, because 'from the last 3 gatherings' also disappears, so the whole header loses a step of structure exactly when the reader is concentrating hardest.
evidence: Compare the two frames: roster has 'Recent 24' + 'Checked in 6' as an adjacent pair; roster-search has 'Checked in 6' alone at x=348 with 'All grades' at x=976. 'RECENT 24 / from the last 3 gatherings' becomes 'RESULTS 9' with the right-hand caption gone.
direction: Keep the row's shape stable across states — hold the chip group's footprint whether it holds one chip or two, so the band does not re-flow under a moving cursor and the search state reads as the same screen filtered rather than a different screen.
